The nephew looked toward him as he went to the door, but gained nothing by it.

“Good night!” his uncle said. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Take a light and show my nephew to his room! And burn him in his bed, if you like,” he added privately, before ringing his little bell again to summon his valet to his own bedroom.

After the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis paced in his loose dressing gown, gently preparing himself for sleep on that hot, still night. His clothing rustled, but his soft slippers made no sound. He moved like an elegant tiger, like one of those irredeemably wicked marquises in fairy tales whose regular transformation into a tiger was either just beginning or just ending.

He crossed and recrossed his luxurious bedroom, revisiting fragments of the day’s journey that returned uninvited: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sinking sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on the rocky height, the little village in the hollow, the peasants by the fountain, and the road mender in his blue cap pointing to the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain recalled the one in Paris: the small bundle on its step, the women bending over it, and the tall man raising his arms and crying, “Dead!”

“I am cool now,” the Marquis said, “and can go to bed.”

Leaving one light burning on the great hearth, he let the thin gauze curtains fall around his bed. As he settled to sleep, he heard the night break its silence with a long sigh.

For three heavy hours, the stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the dark. For three heavy hours, the stable horses rattled their feeding racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound very unlike the one human poets usually assign to owls. Such creatures have a stubborn habit of refusing to say the lines written for them.

For three heavy hours, the chateau’s stone faces, human and lion, stared blindly into the night. Dead darkness covered the landscape and added its silence to the muffling dust of every road. In the burial ground, the small mounds of poor grass were no longer distinguishable. For all anyone could see, the figure on the Cross might have climbed down. In the village, tax collectors and taxpayers slept soundly. Perhaps the starving dreamed of banquets, as starving people do, and of peace and rest, as overworked slaves and harnessed oxen may. The thin villagers slept deeply, fed and free in their dreams.

The daughter lay motionless on the floor; she had fainted. The older woman’s screams and resistance, during which her hair was torn from her scalp, turned the orangutan’s likely peaceful intentions into anger. One forceful stroke of its muscular arm nearly severed her head. The sight of blood intensified its rage into madness. Teeth grinding and eyes blazing, it leaped onto the girl and sank its terrible claws into her throat, maintaining its grip until she died. Its frantic gaze then fell on the head of the bed, above which its master’s horrified, rigid face was just visible. The creature’s fury immediately became fear, no doubt at the memory of the whip it dreaded. Apparently aware that it deserved punishment, it seemed intent on concealing the slaughter. It darted around the room in a frenzy of nervous agitation, overturning and smashing furniture and dragging the mattress off the bed frame. Finally, it grabbed the daughter’s corpse and forced it up the chimney into the position in which it was discovered. Then it seized the older woman’s body and flung it headfirst out of the window.

As the ape came toward the window with its mutilated burden, the sailor recoiled in terror onto the rod. Sliding rather than climbing down, he hurried home at once. His dread of the consequences made him gladly abandon any concern about what would happen to the orangutan. The sounds heard by the party on the staircase were the Frenchman’s horrified, frightened exclamations mingled with the animal’s fiendish babbling.

I have little more to add. The orangutan must have left by the rod immediately before the door was forced, closing the window behind it. Its owner later captured it himself and received a very large payment for it from the Jardin des Plantes. Once we reported the circumstances at the Prefect of Police’s office, with some accompanying remarks from Dupin, Le Don was immediately freed. Friendly though the official felt toward my companion, he could not entirely conceal his irritation at this outcome. He indulged in a few sarcastic observations about how everyone ought to mind their own business.

“Let him talk,” said Dupin, who had chosen not to respond. “Let him speak; it will comfort his conscience. Beating him in his own stronghold is enough for me. Still, his inability to solve the mystery is hardly the astonishing thing he considers it. Our friend the Prefect is, in truth, a little too cunning to be profound.

I next pierced the end of the keg above the pitcher and inserted a soft wooden stopper, shaped to a taper or cone. By pushing it farther in or drawing it out, I soon discovered the precise tightness at which the water leaking through would fill the vessel below in sixty minutes. This was readily and quickly established by observing what fraction of the pitcher filled in a measured interval. With these arrangements complete, the remainder of my design is plain. I laid out my bed upon the car’s floor so that, when reclining, my head rested directly beneath the pitcher’s spout. At the end of an hour, the vessel would plainly overflow; and it would do so through the spout, which sat a little below the rim. Equally plainly, water falling more than four feet from that position must strike my face, waking me instantly even from the deepest possible sleep.

“It was already eleven when I finished these preparations. I went immediately to bed, entirely assured of my contrivance’s success, and in this I suffered no disappointment. Every sixty minutes precisely, my faithful timekeeper awakened me. I emptied the pitcher back through the keg’s bung-hole, attended to the condenser, and returned to bed. These repeated disturbances troubled me even less than I had expected. When I rose at last for the day, the hour was seven, and the sun stood many degrees above my horizon.

“April 3d. The balloon had reached a truly enormous height, and the earth’s apparent curvature was notably greater. A group of black dots upon the ocean beneath me were undoubtedly islands. Far northward, along the horizon’s edge, I could distinguish a narrow white streak of extraordinary brilliance. I readily took it for the southern edge of the ice covering the Polar Sea. My curiosity was powerfully aroused, since I hoped to travel much farther north and might eventually stand directly above the Pole. I now regretted that, should this occur, my immense altitude would prevent the close examination I desired.
